record.ear: Cooler. Wind off the Sound. High 74. Low 58.

lead.headline: Arcade tenants to hold June rent at their counters from 8 a.m. today
lead.deck: No collector has called since May 1; Mr. Raab to sit at the entrance with a summons for costs; Mr. Ewald advises receipts 'in any hand that offers one'
lead.body: The ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade whose notices to vacate were waived by Judge Peter Hanrahan on Monday will have the June rent ready at their counters from 8 a.m. today, in cash. No collector for Signal Ground Rents Inc. has called since May 1, when a man in a grey coat took the May rent at 3:40 p.m. Mr. Raab will sit at the entrance with a summons for costs. Mr. Nathan Ewald advises receipts 'in any hand.'

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,290 night calls on the tone in Queens; 702 posted in Brooklyn
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,290 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,380, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 702. The Brooklyn Courier states that the figure 'is a door's, not ours.'

columns.headline: Steeplechase and Luna Park open the Coney Island season at noon today
columns.body: Steeplechase Park and Luna Park will open the season at Coney Island at noon today, their managements state, with the Cyclone, the Thunderbolt and 31 band stands. The Weather Bureau forecasts a south wind of 12 miles an hour by evening.

columns.headline: Labour the largest party in the new House of Commons, London states
columns.body: The Labour Party will be the largest in the new House of Commons, the London wire states, the count of Thursday's polling having been completed last night. Mr. Stanley Baldwin is expected to resign. The counts were taken by wire and agreed with the paper in every constituency.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-fourth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cool at last. High 74. Saturday. Rent day. Bring a chair.

lead.headline: Arcade waits all day for the rent man, and June's money stays on hold
lead.deck: Ten shops count out their cash into envelopes at eight; Mr. Raab on his folding chair; Duke on duty; twenty to four comes and goes and the grey coat does not
lead.body: The Vantry Arcade had its June rent ready at eight this morning, ten envelopes on ten counters, and nobody came for it. Mr. Raab sat at the entrance on his folding chair with a summons for costs. Alderman Feeney brought Duke. At twenty to four, the hour the grey coat came in May, the whole Arcade looked at the door. A woman came in for cigars. At six the shops counted their envelopes again and locked them up. Signal Ground Rents is now a month behind on its own rent.

columns.headline: Coney opens its season at full volume, and Queens gets the noise for nothing
columns.body: Steeplechase and Luna Park opened at noon with the Cyclone, the Thunderbolt and thirty-one bands, all of them, by our count, playing at once. The Bureau promises a south wind tonight. Woodhaven, which has paid nothing, is advised to open its windows and scream along.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who won the British election?'
columns.body: Sir, Labour, as far as the London wire can tell, and for once the wire and the paper agreed in every seat, which we find suspicious. Mr. Baldwin is expected to resign. The operator rang London on your behalf. London was engaged.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: June brides, and every vow on the house machine
columns.body: Darlings, June is here and the Listening Lady has eleven weddings on her card, nine to be recorded by the church and two by the bride's mother, independently. The Lindberghs set a fashion for silence. Queens has not taken it up. Queens never will.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Woodhaven reports the Cyclone at nine, on the south wind, screams included.

editorial.headline: A decent woman wants no record
editorial.body: Colonel Lindbergh has married Miss Anne Morrow in a house that recorded nothing, at their request, and this paper salutes them. Here is a lesson for the women of Queens. A decent woman wants no record of herself. She does not leave lipstick on the mirrors of public men, nor play their own voices to them in shop windows. Miss Morrow is a decent woman; she is also, we are told, a writer and is learning to fly, which we put down to the influence of the Colonel. The woman called Lilith, this week, did nothing that we could find. We found that suspicious. We were proved right on Thursday, when she did everything.

lead.headline: Coney Island's opening heard in five Queens districts on a south wind
lead.deck: The Exchange logs 214 calls between 9 p.m. and 11 p.m. from Woodhaven, Ozone Park, Richmond Hill, Glendale and Ridgewood; the Cyclone identified 'at the drop'
lead.body: The opening night of the Coney Island season was heard in five Queens districts last night on a south wind of 12 miles an hour, the Queens Exchange states, which logged 214 calls between 9 p.m. and 11 p.m. from Woodhaven, Ozone Park, Richmond Hill, Glendale and Ridgewood. Callers reported band music, a calliope and screaming, the last identified by a Woodhaven subscriber as 'the Cyclone, at the drop.' Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street read 41 cycles throughout.

columns.headline: No collector calls at the Vantry Arcade; June rent held by ten tenants
columns.body: No collector for Signal Ground Rents Inc. called at the Vantry Arcade yesterday between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m., Mr. Oscar Bliss states. The ten tenants hold the June rent. Mr. Nathan Ewald will advise them tomorrow 'as to where it may lawfully wait.'

columns.headline: Dr. Strand to sing at 4 p.m. in the Union Seminary chapel; system off at 3:55
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand will sing 'a short piece, in Welsh, unaccompanied' in the Union Seminary chapel at 4 p.m. today, the seminary states. The chapel's house system will be switched off at its board at 3:55 p.m. at his request. Admission is free.

columns.headline: Board of Elections to count Tuesday's primary by wire before paper
columns.body: The Board of Elections will count Tuesday's Democratic primary for Borough President of Queens by wire first and on paper after, as in November, Chairman Delaney states. Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan are the candidates. Polls open at 6 a.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-fifth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 78. Sunday. Strand sang. Nobody can prove it, which is how he likes it.

lead.headline: Strand sings in Welsh to a dead machine, and the chapel keeps it off the record
lead.deck: Sixty in the pews, the board switched off at five to four, four minutes unaccompanied; one word comes three times and the professor will not tell us which
lead.body: At four this afternoon Dr. Strand stood up in the Union Seminary chapel, the house machine switched off at the board at five to, and sang for about four minutes in Welsh, unaccompanied. Sixty people heard it, and nothing else did. Our man was there. He has no Welsh and no record. He says one word came three times, at the ends of three lines, and the professor's voice went down on it each time. Afterwards Dr. Strand was asked which word. He said, 'It was sung.'

columns.headline: Coney's opening comes through loud and clear in Woodhaven, free of charge
columns.body: Two hundred and fourteen people in five Queens districts rang the Exchange last night to report Coney Island, which they could hear on the south wind and had not paid for. A Woodhaven man identified the Cyclone by the screams. Luna Park is considering sending him a bill.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Twenty-five nights, and the shore men take up whist
columns.body: WORS has been off the band since the seventh of May. Mr. Pike's shore stations still sit from half past ten to midnight. Our man rang at eleven and heard a voice say 'Your lead.' The night clerk says that was not WORS. That was Mr. Pike.

columns.headline: The Pun Derby opens tomorrow, and the field is wide open on every line
columns.body: Tomorrow the Speaker opens its summer Pun Derby to readers. Send your best pun on a postcard, one-cent stamp. Five dollars and a year's Speaker to the weekly winner, judged by the night desk. Puns about the Hum are disqualified, the Hum having heard them all.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nobody in the chapel recorded Dr. Strand. Three people have since hummed it to us. No two agree.

lead.headline: Dr. Strand sings four minutes in Welsh with the chapel's system switched off
lead.deck: About 60 present at Union Seminary; no record made; one word sung three times at the close of three lines; Dr. Strand declines to name it or the piece
lead.body: Dr. Matthias Strand sang for about four minutes in Welsh, unaccompanied, in the Union Seminary chapel at 4 p.m. yesterday, the chapel's house system having been switched off at its board at 3:55 p.m., the seminary states. About 60 persons were present. No record was made. Two seminarians who attended state that one word was sung three times, at the close of three lines. Dr. Strand declined to name the word or the piece, stating that 'it was sung, and that is the record.'

columns.headline: Athletics lead by six games; the Yankees split two with Detroit
columns.body: The Athletics won twice from Boston and lead the American League by six games. The Yankees beat Detroit 7 to 4 at the Stadium on Saturday and lost 3 to 2 yesterday, Mr. Lazzeri hitting a home run. Brooklyn lost to the Giants at the Polo Grounds.

columns.headline: Arcade tenants to pay June rent into the Municipal Court today, counsel states
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald states that the ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade will deposit the June rent with the clerk of the Municipal Court at Long Island City at 10 a.m. today, 'no collector having attended to receive it.' The sum is 412 dollars.

columns.headline: Polls open at 6 a.m. tomorrow in 386 Queens districts for the primary
columns.body: Polls will open at 6 a.m. tomorrow in 386 election districts for the Democratic primary for Borough President, closing at 9 p.m. Each polling place's house system will be read to the Board by wire after closing. Alderman Feeney and Mr. Dolan will vote at 7 a.m.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Stanley Baldwin will resign as Prime Minister tomorrow, the London wire states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 76. Monday. The Pun Derby is open. Pity the postman.

lead.headline: The Pun Derby's off and running, and the mail comes in at full volume
lead.deck: Four hundred and eleven postcards by the noon delivery; the night desk sits as judges; the Hum barred; one entry signed with a hoof
lead.body: The Speaker's summer Pun Derby opened this morning, and by noon the postman had brought four hundred and eleven postcards and asked for a chair. The rules are simple. One pun to a card, one-cent stamp, no puns on the Hum. The night desk judges every Friday, and five dollars and a year's Speaker go to the weekly winner. Early leaders include a Corona woman on valves and a Flushing boy on the operator. One card is signed with a hoof. It is not bad.

columns.headline: Strand's word goes down three times, and nobody gets the replay
columns.body: Two seminarians who heard Dr. Strand sing yesterday say one word came three times at the ends of three lines. They have no Welsh. Neither has the chapel's machine, which was off. The professor says 'it was sung.' We say it was a lot of trouble for one word.

columns.headline: Athletics stretch the lead to six, and the Yankees keep losing the signal
columns.body: Philadelphia won two more from Boston and is six games clear. The Yankees beat Detroit on Saturday and lost on Sunday by a run. Mr. Huggins said nothing about June. The Babe said it was early. It is early. It is also June.

columns.headline: Primary tomorrow: Feeney and Dolan both promise to hear every vote
columns.body: Tomorrow Queens picks a Democrat for Borough President, and the polling places' own machines will be read to the Board by wire before anyone counts a ballot. Alderman Feeney will vote at seven with Duke. Mr. Dolan will vote at seven with Mr. Senn, who will log it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Baldwin goes tomorrow. Britain will hear it from the King, who will hear it first.

record.ear: Fair. High 79. Low 62. Polls open 6 a.m. to 9 p.m.

lead.headline: Queens votes today in a primary for Borough President; count by wire tonight
lead.deck: 386 districts; Alderman Feeney and Former Commissioner Dolan the candidates; Chairman Delaney to read the polling places' systems from 9:15 p.m.; paper count to follow 'as a check'
lead.body: Enrolled Democrats in Queens vote today between 6 a.m. and 9 p.m. in 386 election districts to choose a candidate for Borough President, Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan standing. The Board of Elections will read each polling place's house system by wire from 9:15 p.m., Chairman Delaney states, and the ballots will be counted on paper afterward 'as a check.' In November the two counts differed by 1,912 votes. The Chairman states that 'the clerks have since been retrained.'

columns.headline: Ten Arcade tenants deposit 412 dollars of June rent with the Municipal Court
columns.body: The ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade deposited 412 dollars of June rent with the clerk of the Municipal Court at Long Island City at 10:20 a.m. yesterday, the clerk states, 'to the credit of Signal Ground Rents Inc., when it calls.'

columns.headline: No decision on the Riverhead seal before the recess; Mr. Gorman attends
columns.body: The clerk of the Appellate Division states that no decision on Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Riverhead record will be handed down before the summer recess. Mr. Gorman attended yesterday's sitting, his thirty-fourth, and asked when the recess begins.

columns.headline: Mr. Baldwin resigns today; Mr. MacDonald expected to be sent for
columns.body: Mr. Stanley Baldwin will go to Windsor today to resign as Prime Minister, the London wire states, and Mr. Ramsay MacDonald is expected to be sent for. The audience is not to be recorded, 'as is customary,' the Palace states.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-seventh night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 79. Tuesday. Vote early. The machine is listening anyway.

lead.headline: Queens casts its ballot, and every polling booth takes it down word for word
lead.deck: Feeney votes at seven, and Duke is turned away at the curtain; Dolan votes at seven while Mr. Senn logs it; the wire counts tonight and the paper counts after
lead.body: Queens Democrats picked a Borough President today in three hundred and eighty-six schools, firehouses and barbers' back rooms, each of them wired, each of them listening. Alderman Feeney voted at seven in Astoria, and Duke was turned away by a clerk who said the booth was for one. Mr. Dolan voted at seven in Long Island City while Mr. Senn logged 'a curtain, a pencil, nothing else.' Tonight the Board counts by wire. In November that went wrong by nineteen hundred votes.

columns.headline: Gorman's thirty-fourth sitting, and the court goes on summer hold
columns.body: The Appellate Division will rise for the summer before it rules on Mr. Gorman's eleven seconds. Mr. Gorman asked when the recess begins. He was told. He has written the date inside his hat. He will be there the day it ends, with sandwiches.

columns.headline: Arcade pays its rent to the court, and the clerk takes the call for the company
columns.body: The ten shops took their June money to the Municipal Court clerk yesterday, four hundred and twelve dollars, to wait until Signal Ground Rents comes to ask for it. The clerk signed the receipt himself. It is the first receipt this year with a name on it.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can my vote be overheard?'
columns.body: Madam, yes. Every polling place in Queens is wired, and the Board will hear the machines tonight before it counts the paper. But a pencil makes no noise worth hearing. Do not say the name aloud. Several in Corona did this morning. Several in Corona always do.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: First wire returns at ten: Feeney ahead. Second wire returns at eleven: still Feeney, by less. We went to press.

lead.headline: Wire count gives Mr. Feeney the primary by 212 votes; paper count incomplete
lead.deck: Feeney 31,418, Dolan 31,206 by the polling places' systems; paper count in 340 of 386 districts gives Mr. Dolan a lead of 57; Mr. Dolan asks a recount by wire
lead.body: The Board of Elections' count by wire of yesterday's Democratic primary for Borough President gives Alderman John Feeney 31,418 votes and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan 31,206, a margin of 212, Chairman Delaney announced at 2:10 a.m. The count on paper, completed in 340 of 386 districts by 6 a.m., gives Mr. Dolan a lead of 57. Mr. Dolan has asked that the polling places' systems be read a second time. The Board will recount by wire from 9 a.m. tomorrow.

columns.headline: Mr. MacDonald accepts the King's commission to form a government
columns.body: Mr. Ramsay MacDonald accepted the King's commission to form a government at Windsor yesterday, the London wire states, after Mr. Stanley Baldwin's resignation in the morning. Mr. MacDonald's statement outside the castle, recorded by the British wire, runs 31 seconds.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin to fly round the world in August, Dr. Eckener states
columns.body: Dr. Hugo Eckener stated at Friedrichshafen yesterday that the Graf Zeppelin will attempt a flight round the world in August, beginning and ending at Lakehurst, with stops at Friedrichshafen, Tokyo and Los Angeles. The Navy's station at Lakehurst will 'listen her round.'

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin to measure the tone from a rowboat on the Sound on Saturday
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin will measure the tone from a rowboat on Long Island Sound off College Point on Saturday night at nine stations a third of a mile apart, his office states. Queens Light & Power states that the Sound 'is not on its system.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-eighth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 81. Wednesday. The wire says Feeney. The paper says Dolan. Duke says nothing.

lead.headline: Wire calls it for Feeney, paper calls it for Dolan, and Queens is on hold
lead.deck: Two hundred and twelve one way by the machines, fifty-seven the other by the pencils; Mr. Dolan wants the machines played again; Mr. Delaney's clerks have been retrained, he says
lead.body: At ten past two this morning Mr. Delaney of the Board of Elections announced that the polling places' machines had nominated Alderman Feeney by two hundred and twelve votes. By six the paper ballots, mostly counted, had nominated Mr. Dolan by fifty-seven. Both candidates have claimed victory, and only one of them can be right. Mr. Dolan has asked for the machines to be played again, and the Board will do it tomorrow. Mr. Feeney says the wire never lies. In November it lied by nineteen hundred.

columns.headline: Zeppelin to go round the world in August, and Lakehurst takes the long call
columns.body: Dr. Eckener says the Graf Zeppelin will fly round the world in August, from Lakehurst and back by way of Germany, Tokyo and Los Angeles. The Navy says it will listen her round. Our office boy has asked for a bigger map and more pins.

columns.headline: Rastin rows out Saturday, and the light company says the Sound's off its line
columns.body: Dr. Rastin is taking his meter to sea on Saturday night, in a rowboat off College Point, to see whether the tone carries over water. Queens Light & Power says the Sound is not on its system. The Sound has not commented.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: two thousand cards, one horse, and the night desk loses its voice
columns.body: Two thousand and six postcards by tonight, and the night desk has read them all aloud. The leader so far is a Flushing boy: 'Why is the operator never lonely? She has too many connections.' The horse has entered again. The judges rule on Friday.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Dolan's listener logged the counting room overnight: 'clerks, coffee, two hundred and twelve, nothing else.'

lead.headline: Vantry estate sells the Arcade's ground rent outright to Signal Ground Rents
lead.deck: Deed recorded at the Register's office, Jamaica, at 3:12 p.m.; dated May 31; consideration 'one dollar and other value'; executed for the company by a rubber stamp, no signature appearing
lead.body: A deed conveying the ground rent of the Vantry Arcade outright from the executors of the Vantry estate to Signal Ground Rents Inc. was recorded at the Register's office in Jamaica at 3:12 p.m. yesterday, the Register states. It is dated May 31 and states a consideration of 'one dollar and other value.' The executors sign by hand. The company's execution is a rubber stamp reading 'Signal Ground Rents Inc., by its Secretary,' no signature appearing. The address given is the company's post office box.

columns.headline: Board to recount the primary by wire from 9 a.m.; paper count complete
columns.body: The Board of Elections will read all 386 polling places' systems a second time from 9 a.m. today, Chairman Delaney states. The paper count, completed at 4 p.m. yesterday, gives Mr. Dolan 31,291 and Alderman Feeney 31,253, a lead for Mr. Dolan of 38.

columns.headline: Mr. Feeney and Mr. Dolan to debate at Flushing tonight as arranged
columns.body: Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan will debate at the Flushing High School at 8 p.m. today as arranged on May 23, both campaigns state, the subject being amended from 'the half cent' to 'the count.' Mr. Dolan's listener will attend.

columns.headline: Mrs. Grieve publishes her list of 38 records; No. 23 not among them
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve has published the list of 38 records to be sealed in her capsule at the Flushing Free Library at 11 a.m. on June 15. Record No. 23 is not on it. Mr. Cyril Abbot has not replied to a fifth letter.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the twenty-ninth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 80. Thursday. The Arcade has been sold. By a stamp. To a box.

lead.headline: Arcade's deed is signed by a rubber stamp, and nobody's on the other end
lead.deck: The Vantry executors sign in ink; Signal Ground Rents signs in rubber, 'by its Secretary'; the Secretary has no name and the address is the post box nobody rents
lead.body: The Vantry Arcade, ground rent and all, now belongs outright to Signal Ground Rents Inc., which bought it for a dollar and other value. The deed went on the books in Jamaica yesterday. The executors of the Vantry estate signed it in ink. The company signed it with a rubber stamp reading 'by its Secretary,' and the Secretary did not add a name. The address is the post box Mr. Raab has found 'not rented' four times. The Arcade has a new landlord. It had this one before.

columns.headline: Recount by wire today, and the paper count digs in at thirty-eight
columns.body: The paper ballots are all counted now, and Mr. Dolan leads by thirty-eight. The machines said Feeney by two hundred and twelve. Today the Board plays the machines again. If they agree with themselves, Queens will have two answers, each held with total confidence.

columns.headline: Feeney and Dolan meet tonight to argue a count neither of them can hear
columns.body: Tonight at Flushing High School the two candidates debate again. The subject was the half cent. It is now the count. Mr. Senn will log it. Duke will attend. The Commission rules on the half cent on Tuesday, so naturally nobody will be talking about it.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who do I pay my rent to now?'
columns.body: Sir, if you are in the Arcade, to the Municipal Court clerk, who is holding it for a company that signs with a stamp. If you are anywhere else, to your landlord. If your landlord signs with a stamp, ring us. We would like to compare stamps.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The recount by wire stood at Feeney by 209 at the halfway mark. The paper ballots were not consulted.

lead.headline: About 1,400 hear the candidates debate the count at Flushing for 94 minutes
lead.deck: The school's system records the evening; Mr. Dolan calls the wire count 'a machine's opinion'; Alderman Feeney calls the paper count 'a pencil's'; recount at Feeney by 209 with 191 districts read
lead.body: About 1,400 persons heard Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan debate at the Flushing High School last night for 94 minutes, the school's house system recording. Mr. Dolan called the count by wire 'a machine's opinion of a pencil.' Alderman Feeney called the paper count 'a pencil's opinion of itself.' The Board's recount by wire stood at Feeney by 209 with 191 of 386 districts read. Mr. Senn's log of the evening reads 'two men, a dog, rain on the skylight.'

columns.headline: Experts' committee in Paris to sign its reparations report today
columns.body: The committee of experts on German reparations, Mr. Owen D. Young presiding, will sign its report in Paris today, the Paris wire states. The signing is to be recorded 'in five languages, by five machines,' the committee states.

columns.headline: Register's clerk states a man in a grey coat examined the Arcade deed
columns.body: Mr. Lionel Daubney, clerk in the Register's office at Jamaica, states that a man of about fifty in a grey coat, without a hat, asked to see the Vantry Arcade deed at 4 p.m. yesterday, read it through, said 'Correct,' and left.

columns.headline: Public Service Commission to rule on the half cent at 10 a.m. Tuesday
columns.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey will read the decision on Alderman John Feeney's petition against the half-cent increase in the light rate at 10 a.m. Tuesday, the Commission states. The half cent collected since May 1 is held in a separate account.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirtieth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Showers. High 72. Friday. Party Line's tenth. The Pun Derby's first.

lead.headline: Feeney and Dolan argue the count, and Flushing gets crossed wires
lead.deck: A machine's opinion of a pencil against a pencil's opinion of itself; fourteen hundred in the hall, rain on the skylight, Duke under the table; the recount stands at two hundred and nine
lead.body: Last night at Flushing High School Mr. Dolan said the wire count was a machine's opinion of a pencil, and Alderman Feeney said the paper count was a pencil's opinion of itself, and fourteen hundred people sat in a hall loud with rain for an hour and a half trying to decide which was ruder. Duke slept under the table. Mr. Senn logged it. The recount by wire, half done, has Feeney by two hundred and nine. The paper ballots have not been asked their opinion again.

columns.headline: Party Line's tenth Friday, and the stool starts taking messages
columns.body: Ten Fridays. Party Line was at the parcel window at four, by way of the stool. No tin from Corona. Somebody had left a note on the cushion, 'For P.L., in case,' with nothing in it. She sat on the note. Sergeant Moran says the warrant is current.

columns.headline: Pun Derby, week one: the operator's connections carry the day
columns.body: First week's winner of the Pun Derby, out of four thousand cards: the Flushing boy, Master Albert Nolan, aged eleven, with the lonely operator and her connections. Five dollars and a year's Speaker. The horse came second. The horse has asked to see the judges.

columns.headline: Grey coat reads the deed in Jamaica, and says the one word he knows
columns.body: A man in a grey coat walked into the Register's office yesterday at four, read the Arcade deed through, said 'Correct' and walked out. The clerk did not stop him, there being no law against agreeing with a deed. Mr. Raab was in Elmhurst at the time.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: No tin for Party Line. She took the empty note to the warm end.

lead.headline: Week's count: recount by wire gives Feeney 211; paper gives Dolan 38
lead.deck: The two counts differ by 249 votes in 23 districts; Chairman Delaney to sit Monday 'on which count is the count'; Mr. Dolan's counsel to apply to the Supreme Court
lead.body: The Board of Elections completed its recount by wire of Tuesday's Democratic primary for Borough President at 5:40 p.m. yesterday, giving Alderman John Feeney a margin of 211, one fewer than on Tuesday night. The paper count gives Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan a margin of 38. The counts differ by 249 votes in 23 districts. Chairman Delaney states that the Board will sit on Monday 'to decide which count is the count.' Mr. Dolan's counsel states that he will apply to the Supreme Court.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,240 night calls on the tone in Queens; 740 on the Brooklyn door
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,240 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,290, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 740. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles.

columns.headline: Licences: 1,602 granted; 4,105 forms returned; three weeks to July 1
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 258 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 1,602 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms, 4,105 have been returned. The Astoria ferry's application remains under review. Licences are required from July 1.

columns.headline: Experts sign the reparations report in Paris; payments over 59 years
columns.body: The committee of experts on reparations signed its report in Paris yesterday afternoon, the Paris wire states, proposing annual payments by Germany over 59 years. Mr. Owen D. Young signed first. The five records of the signing are said to agree.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the tenth Friday without one, the supervisor states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 75. Saturday. June, weddings, and a voice from 1924.

lead.headline: Bride's late father gives his toast on the record, and the breakfast goes quiet
lead.deck: Miss Rosa Kiernan of Astoria weds at St. Joseph's; at the breakfast her mother plays the disc her father made at her first communion; forty guests and one long pause
lead.body: Miss Rosa Kiernan of 30th Avenue, Astoria, married Mr. Thomas Wylde at St. Joseph's this morning, and at the wedding breakfast, between the ham and the cake, her mother put a record on the gramophone. Her father, a motorman, made it in 1924 at her first communion party, two years before he died. He says, 'And when she marries, God help the fellow, I want to be asked.' Forty guests heard him ask. The groom said yes on his own behalf. Then they cut the cake.

columns.headline: Recount comes through one vote lighter, and the paper still won't pick up
columns.body: The machines were played again and Mr. Feeney won by two hundred and eleven, which is one fewer than the machines said on Tuesday. Nobody knows where the vote went. The paper still says Mr. Dolan by thirty-eight. Mr. Delaney sits Monday to decide which is the count.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? A month of dead air, and the map is gathering dust
columns.body: WORS has now been silent a month, since the evening of the seventh of May. The office boy's pin ninety-seven stands in the river, dusted daily. Mr. Pike's night clerk has finished the whist season. He says June is quiet. He says it carefully.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: eleven weddings, nine machines, one gramophone that won
columns.body: Darlings, eleven weddings this Saturday and the Listening Lady has heard nine of them already, the churches being prompt. The best was not in a church at all but on a gramophone at an Astoria breakfast, of which enough is said above. Bring a handkerchief. She did.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Rastin has pushed off from College Point with a meter, a lantern and an oarsman who asked for his money first.

editorial.headline: Clean streets, safe wives, and a laundress unpaid
editorial.body: Mr. Ezra Coyle, who opened his campaign for borough president this week on the platform Clean Streets, Safe Wives and No More Lilith, has the support of this newspaper and of every man who wants his wife at home by nine. At a dance at Steeplechase Park on Thursday, however, Mr. Coyle was overheard telling a lady in black that he has not paid his laundress since 1927 because 'a widow will wash for the honour of it,' and the band, which had been told the words in advance, played them back to him as a foxtrot. The laundress has been paid. Mr. Coyle remains our candidate. We ask only that he wash his own platform.

lead.headline: Dr. Rastin reads 41 cycles at each of nine stations on the Sound from a rowboat
lead.deck: Measurements between 1:10 a.m. and 3:50 a.m. off College Point, the farthest three miles out; the oarsman states he 'did not need the meter'
lead.body: Dr. Emil Rastin measured the tone from a rowboat on Long Island Sound off College Point between 1:10 a.m. and 3:50 a.m. yesterday, reading 41 cycles at each of nine stations, the farthest three miles from shore, his office states. The oarsman, Mr. Pat Mulry of College Point, states that he 'heard it the whole way out and did not need the meter.' Queens Light & Power states that the Sound is not on its system. Dr. Rastin will publish his readings on Thursday.

columns.headline: Late motorman's record played at an Astoria wedding breakfast
columns.body: A record made in 1924 by the late Mr. Daniel Kiernan, motorman, was played at the wedding breakfast of his daughter, Miss Rosa Kiernan, and Mr. Thomas Wylde, at 30th Avenue, Astoria, yesterday. Forty guests attended. The record runs 52 seconds.

columns.headline: About 600,000 at Coney Island; the Exchange logs 96 calls from Woodhaven
columns.body: About 600,000 persons visited Coney Island yesterday, the police state, the warmest Saturday of the season. The Queens Exchange logged 96 calls from Woodhaven and Ozone Park between 8 p.m. and 10 p.m. reporting 'Coney Island,' the wind being southerly.

columns.headline: Brooklyn Courier states that the Sound 'is not a Brooklyn matter'
columns.body: The Brooklyn Courier states in a notice signed by Mr. Ambrose Tully that it will print no account of Dr. Rastin's measurements on the Sound, 'the Sound not being a Brooklyn matter, and the tone not being one at all.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-second night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Calm. High 77. Sunday. Rastin went to sea. The Hum went with him.

lead.headline: Rastin rows three miles out, and the Hum stays on the same frequency
lead.deck: Nine readings off College Point, nine forty-ones; the oarsman wants to know why he needed a professor; Brooklyn rules the Sound out of bounds
lead.body: Dr. Rastin went out on the Sound last night in a rowboat with a meter, a lantern and Mr. Pat Mulry at the oars, to find out whether the Hum stops at the water's edge. It does not. He read forty-one at the shore, forty-one a mile out, and forty-one at three miles, where Mr. Mulry shipped his oars and asked whether they had gone far enough. They had. Mr. Mulry says he could have told the Doctor that for a dollar, without the boat.

columns.headline: Courier rules the Sound out of bounds, and Mr. Tully stays on dry land
columns.body: Mr. Tully of the Brooklyn Courier says the Sound is not a Brooklyn matter and the tone is not a matter at all. The Sound touches Brooklyn at several points. Mr. Tully touches nothing that hums. Brooklyn's door count stands at seven hundred and forty.

columns.headline: Coney's crowds come through in Woodhaven again, and the reception's free
columns.body: Six hundred thousand went to Coney yesterday and ninety-six Woodhaven households heard them on the south wind without leaving home. A Woodhaven grocer has put chairs on his back step and charges a penny a seat. Luna Park is livid.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: the horse's owner calls the judges, and gets a hoarse reply
columns.body: The horse's owner, Mr. Kehoe of the Steinway coal yard, writes that the hoof was no joke. His entry: 'Why did the mare refuse the telephone? She was a little hoarse.' The judges have filed it. Week two opens Monday.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Mulry has been paid. He asks whether the Doctor would like to try Jamaica Bay.

lead.headline: Ice to cost 55 cents the hundredweight from today, the three companies state
lead.deck: The summer price, up ten cents from the spring; the 25-pound piece at 15 cents; Mr. Gustave Pohl cites oats and the heat of May 28; Duchess to work the Steinway route
lead.body: The Astoria Lake, Jamaica Pond and Flushing Bay ice companies will charge 55 cents the hundredweight from today, up from 45, and 15 cents the 25-pound piece, the companies state in a joint notice. Mr. Gustave Pohl of the Astoria Lake Company states that the price reflects 'oats, the heat of May 28, and the shortage on the river.' The 11 extra wagons will remain on the road until September. Mr. Pohl states that Duchess will work the Steinway route 'for the summer, in a hat.'

columns.headline: Athletics lead by seven; the Yankees win three of four from Cleveland
columns.body: The Athletics beat Chicago twice and lead the American League by seven games. The Yankees won three of four from Cleveland at the Stadium, Mr. Ruth hitting home runs on Saturday and yesterday. Brooklyn beat Pittsburgh at Ebbets Field.

columns.headline: Board of Elections sits at 10 a.m. to rule on which primary count stands
columns.body: The Board of Elections will sit at 10 a.m. today on the two counts of the Democratic primary for Borough President, Chairman Delaney states, the wire giving Alderman Feeney 211 and the paper giving Mr. Dolan 38. Counsel for both candidates will attend.

columns.headline: Commission to rule tomorrow on the half cent held since May 1
columns.body: The Public Service Commission will rule at 10 a.m. tomorrow on Alderman John Feeney's petition against the half-cent increase in the domestic light rate in Astoria and Steinway, Commissioner Maurice Lacey reading. About 4,100 dollars is held in the separate account, the company states.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-third night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 82. Monday. Ice up a dime. Chip carefully.

lead.headline: Ice men raise the pitch to fifty-five, and the drip tray changes its tune
lead.deck: A dime more the hundredweight from this morning; Mr. Pohl blames oats, May and the river; Duchess will wear a hat; Queens will chip smaller
lead.body: Ice went up a dime the hundredweight this morning, to fifty-five cents, and a twenty-five pound piece is fifteen. The three companies say it is oats, the heat at the end of May and a shortage on the river, and the oats at least are true. Queens will chip smaller and drink warmer. Mr. Pohl says Duchess will work the Steinway route all summer in a straw hat with holes for her ears. The hat is free. The ice is not.

columns.headline: Athletics run it to seven, and the Babe hits two to keep the Yankees in range
columns.body: Philadelphia beat Chicago twice and is seven games clear. The Yankees took three of four from Cleveland, and the Babe hit one on Saturday and one on Sunday, which is the sound we have been waiting for. Mr. Huggins has started saying it is only June.

columns.headline: Board sits today to pick a count, and each candidate brings his own
columns.body: Mr. Delaney's Board sits at ten this morning to decide whether the wire or the paper nominated the Democrat. Mr. Feeney's counsel carries the wire count. Mr. Dolan's counsel carries the paper. The clerks, who made both, have been told to bring lunch.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'May I telephone the ice man?'
columns.body: Madam, you may, if he has a telephone, which he has not. The ice man is reached by the card in your window saying 25, 50 or 100. Turn it the right way up. A Sunnyside woman has had a hundredweight a day since April, holding it upside down.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Board sat four hours and sent both counts to the Supreme Court. Neither count objected.

lead.headline: Board of Elections sends both primary counts to the Supreme Court
lead.deck: Chairman Delaney: the Board 'has two counts and no rule for choosing'; Justice Arthur Lowry to hear counsel on June 17; the polling places' records sealed at the Board
lead.body: The Board of Elections sat for four hours yesterday on the two counts of the Democratic primary for Borough President and referred both to the Supreme Court, Chairman Delaney stating that the Board 'has two counts and no rule for choosing between them.' Justice Arthur Lowry will hear counsel at Long Island City on June 17. The house records of all 386 polling places have been sealed at the Board's offices. Alderman Feeney states that he 'trusts the wire.' Mr. Dolan states that he 'trusts the pencil.'

columns.headline: Commission to read its decision on the light rate at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Commissioner Maurice Lacey will read the Public Service Commission's decision on the half-cent increase in the domestic light rate at 10 a.m. today, the Commission states. Alderman John Feeney will attend. Queens Light & Power will be represented by its counsel, Mr. Harlan Voss.

columns.headline: Grieve capsule to be sealed Saturday at 11 a.m.; Mr. Abbot 'not invited'
columns.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve states that the capsule will be sealed at the Flushing Free Library at 11 a.m. on Saturday with 38 records, and that Mr. Cyril Abbot of the Phonautograph Society 'is not invited, but may attend.' Record No. 23 remains in Mr. Abbot's keeping.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its eleventh week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27, containing the word 'resent,' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its eleventh week. Senator Rufus Keel has asked after it a third time this month.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-fourth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 84. Tuesday. The half cent comes home. Some of it.

lead.headline: Half cent comes back down the line, and Feeney's brief pays out in July
lead.deck: Commissioner Lacey lets the new rate stand from tomorrow but sends six weeks of half cents home on the July bill; no interest, at the company's rate or anyone's; Feeney claims victory
lead.body: At ten this morning Commissioner Lacey ruled that Queens Light & Power may charge seven and a half cents from tomorrow, but that every half cent kept in the separate account since the first of May goes back to Astoria and Steinway as a credit on the July bill. No interest. Alderman Feeney, who asked in thirty-one pages for interest at the company's own rate, got none of it and called it a victory anyway. The company called it a decision. Duke barked once, and was asked to leave.

columns.headline: Board hangs up on both counts, and Justice Lowry takes the call
columns.body: Mr. Delaney's Board sat four hours yesterday, decided it had two counts and no rule for choosing, and passed both to Justice Lowry, who hears them on Monday. Mr. Feeney trusts the wire. Mr. Dolan trusts the pencil. The voters have been asked to wait.

columns.headline: Grieve seals Saturday, and Abbot's invitation is lost in the post
columns.body: Mrs. Grieve seals her thirty-eight records at the Flushing library on Saturday. Mr. Abbot is not invited but may attend, which is how she puts it. No. 23 stays on Mr. Abbot's shelf. Neither of them has spoken to the other since April.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'How much is my half cent?'
columns.body: Sir, it depends how much light you burned since May. A Steinway family with two lamps and a set may expect about nineteen cents on the July bill. The operator is taking hers in coal. Mr. Feeney says you are welcome.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Commission's finding repeats that the tone is 'not shown to be carried by the company's conductors.' Nobody had asked.

lead.headline: Commission lets the new light rate stand; half cent since May 1 to be credited
lead.deck: Commissioner Lacey reads at 10:04 a.m.; the increase allowed from today; about 4,100 dollars to be credited on the July bills without interest; Commissioner Ruehl dissents
lead.body: The Public Service Commission ruled yesterday that Queens Light & Power may charge 7.5 cents the kilowatt-hour for domestic light in Astoria and Steinway from today, and that the half cent held in a separate account since May 1, about 4,100 dollars, be credited to subscribers on the July bills without interest, Commissioner Maurice Lacey reading at 10:04 a.m. Commissioner Otto Ruehl dissented. The finding repeats that the tone 'is not shown to be carried by the company's conductors.'

columns.headline: Hollander Valve & Supply Co. of Jamaica files a petition in bankruptcy
columns.body: The Hollander Valve & Supply Co. of Jamaica Avenue, Jamaica, wholesalers of household valves to about 300 Queens grocers, filed a voluntary petition in bankruptcy in the Federal Court at Brooklyn yesterday, stating liabilities of 84,000 dollars. About 61,000 valves are in its warehouse.

columns.headline: Mr. Pruett's trial on June 18; Mrs. Dorr to give evidence for the State
columns.body: Mrs. Agnes Dorr of No. 4 will give evidence for the State at Mr. Gideon Pruett's trial in Special Sessions on June 18, the District Attorney states. Two of the four tenants who moved out will also attend. The Pruett system is to be played to the court.

columns.headline: Process server finds the post box named in the Arcade deed 'not rented'
columns.body: Mr. Raab, process server, tried the address given in the Vantry Arcade deed, the post office box of Signal Ground Rents Inc., yesterday with a summons for costs, and found it 'not rented,' his fifth attempt. The June rent remains with the court clerk.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-fifth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 85. Wednesday. Valves cheap, valve man broke.

lead.headline: Hollander's valves burn out, and Jamaica's biggest dealer goes dark
lead.deck: Eighty-four thousand dollars owing and sixty-one thousand tubes in the warehouse; three hundred grocers wonder where the next six for a dollar will come from; the receiver says 'from me'
lead.body: The Hollander Valve & Supply Co. of Jamaica, which sells a valve to nearly every grocer in Queens who sells a valve, went into bankruptcy yesterday owing eighty-four thousand dollars. It has sixty-one thousand valves in a warehouse on Jamaica Avenue and nobody to pay for them. Mr. Hollander says the trouble began when he bought dear from Newark after the January fire and then had to sell cheap. The receiver will sell the stock. Grocers are advised to look sad and bring a cart.

columns.headline: Pruett goes to trial Tuesday, and Mrs. Dorr has rehearsed with the walls
columns.body: Mr. Pruett's trial is set for next Tuesday, and Mrs. Dorr of No. 4 will testify for the State. She has been practising aloud. Her walls, she says, have heard it all already. The court will play the cellar's machine. Mr. Pruett's counsel has asked that it be played softly.

columns.headline: Raab rings the post box a fifth time, and the box still isn't home
columns.body: Mr. Raab took a summons for costs to the address on the Arcade deed, which is the post box, which is not rented. Fifth time. The clerk at the post office has started saying good morning before Mr. Raab can ask.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: week two's leader married a lineman, and he's always tied up
columns.body: Week two's leader is a Woodside wife: 'I married a lineman. Every time I want him, he's tied up.' Six thousand cards so far. Mr. Kehoe's horse has entered three more times. The judges have asked Mr. Kehoe to have a word with the horse.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Valves at ninety cents the six in Jamaica by four o'clock. The receiver has not sold one yet. Grocers are guessing.

lead.headline: Valves fall to 90 cents the six after the Hollander failure; receiver appointed
lead.deck: Judge Albert Strell names Mr. Reuben Tate receiver; the 61,000 valves to be sold in lots from Monday; long-life grade at 20 cents; grocers' association asks members not to hoard
lead.body: Valves sold at 90 cents the six at Jamaica and Long Island City yesterday, down ten cents, after the failure of the Hollander Valve & Supply Co., the Queens Retail Grocers' Association states. Judge Albert Strell of the Federal Court at Brooklyn appointed Mr. Reuben Tate receiver at 3 p.m. Mr. Tate will sell the 61,000 valves in the Jamaica Avenue warehouse in lots of 600 from Monday. Long-life valves were quoted at 20 cents each. Fresh eggs were unchanged at 36 cents the dozen.

columns.headline: Schools close tomorrow; Newtown High School to graduate 412 at 10 a.m.
columns.body: The public schools of Queens close for the summer tomorrow, the Board of Education states. Newtown High School will graduate 412 seniors at 10 a.m. in its auditorium, the commencement to be recorded by the school's house system and kept 'for the class's reunion in 1954.'

columns.headline: Justice Lowry to hear the primary counts Monday; neither candidate to speak
columns.body: Justice Arthur Lowry will hear counsel on the two counts of the Democratic primary for Borough President at 10 a.m. Monday at Long Island City. The sealed polling-place records will be brought from the Board under guard. Neither candidate is to address the court.

columns.headline: Mr. Abbot replies to Mrs. Grieve's fifth letter 'by return, in one line'
columns.body: Mr. Cyril Abbot of the Phonautograph Society states that he replied yesterday to Mrs. Ottoline Grieve's fifth letter concerning Record No. 23, 'by return, in one line.' Mrs. Grieve states that she has received the line and that No. 23 'is not among the 38.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-sixth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 83. Thursday. School's out tomorrow. Mothers, brace.

lead.headline: Newtown's class of '29 graduates tomorrow, and every name goes on the record
lead.deck: Four hundred and twelve seniors, one machine, a principal who reads slowly; discs of each name at a quarter apiece; the band has practised the march twice and will play it once
lead.body: Tomorrow at ten Newtown High School graduates four hundred and twelve boys and girls, and the school's machine will take down every name as Dr. Wendell Pryor reads it. Dr. Pryor reads slowly. Allow two hours. Parents may buy a disc of their child's name being called, with the applause after, for a quarter, and the school has had six hundred orders. The class will hear itself again in 1954, at the twenty-fifth reunion, which most of them think is a joke. It is not.

columns.headline: Valves drop a dime at the bankruptcy, and the grocers see the light
columns.body: Six for ninety cents in Jamaica yesterday, a dime off, because the Hollander warehouse is full and the receiver wants it empty by July. The Grocers' Association asks its members not to hoard. Its members have asked the Association where it bought its own.

columns.headline: Abbot answers Grieve in one line, and the line is busy
columns.body: Mr. Abbot has answered Mrs. Grieve's fifth letter about No. 23 by return, in a single line. Mrs. Grieve says she has it. Neither will say what it says. No. 23 will not be in Saturday's capsule. The capsule will be sealed regardless.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Thirty-six nights, and the shore men want their evenings back
columns.body: Mr. Pike's shore men have sat thirty-six nights from half past ten to midnight with nothing on sixteen-ten. They have asked for their evenings back. Mr. Pike says not yet. Our office boy reports that pin ninety-seven has begun to rust.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Senate vault still holds 'resent.' Senator Keel has asked a third time. The vault has not replied either.

lead.headline: Newtown High School graduates 412 today; the record to be kept until 1954
lead.deck: Exercises at 10 a.m.; Dr. Wendell Pryor to read every name; 600 discs ordered at 25 cents; the public schools of Queens close at noon for the summer
lead.body: Newtown High School will graduate 412 seniors at 10 a.m. today in its auditorium at Elmhurst, Dr. Wendell Pryor, principal, reading every name. The exercises will be recorded by the school's house system and the record kept in the principal's safe for the class's twenty-fifth reunion in 1954. Parents have ordered about 600 discs of single names at 25 cents each. The public schools of Queens close at noon. The Board of Education states that about 118,000 pupils are affected.

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin publishes his Sound readings: nine stations, 41 cycles at each
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin published his readings from Long Island Sound yesterday: nine stations off College Point between 1:10 a.m. and 3:50 a.m. on Saturday, 41 cycles at each. He states that he will measure from Jamaica Bay in July 'if a boat can be had.'

columns.headline: Valve receiver's first sale on Monday; about 600 grocers apply for lots
columns.body: Mr. Reuben Tate, receiver of the Hollander Valve & Supply Co., states that about 600 grocers have applied for lots at Monday's sale at the Jamaica Avenue warehouse, twice the firm's number of customers. Valves held at 90 cents the six yesterday.

columns.headline: President Hoover to sign the farm marketing bill tomorrow, Washington states
columns.body: President Hoover will sign the Agricultural Marketing Act tomorrow, creating a Federal Farm Board with a fund of 500 million dollars, the Washington wire states. The signing is to be recorded by the White House system 'at the President's desk.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-seventh night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 80. Friday. Eleven Fridays. School's out. The cat stays in.

lead.headline: Pryor reads 412 names, and Queens' schools ring off for the summer
lead.deck: Two hours and eleven minutes at Newtown, every name taken down with its applause; the march played once, as promised; a hundred and eighteen thousand children let out at noon
lead.body: Dr. Pryor read four hundred and twelve names this morning at Newtown, slowly, and the machine took every one, with the applause after and the cough in row nine during the M's. It took two hours and eleven minutes. Then the band played the march once, as promised, and at noon the schools of Queens let out a hundred and eighteen thousand children at once, into the streets, the parks and, by three, Coney Island. The discs go out next week. 1954 has been told to expect them.

columns.headline: Party Line's eleventh Friday, and the schoolchildren come to watch
columns.body: Eleven Fridays. The schools let out at noon, and by four there were nine children at the Exchange's parcel window to watch Party Line wait. She waited. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran says the warrant is current. The children were shown out at five, quietly.

columns.headline: Pun Derby, week two: the lineman's wife ties it up
columns.body: Week two goes to Mrs. Hilda Brandt of Woodside, who married a lineman and finds him always tied up. Five dollars and a year's Speaker. Mr. Kehoe's horse placed second again. Mr. Kehoe says the judges are prejudiced against hooves.

columns.headline: Grieve seals her capsule tomorrow, and keeps a sleeve on hold for No. 23
columns.body: Tomorrow at eleven Mrs. Grieve seals thirty-eight records at the Flushing Free Library. She has kept a thirty-ninth sleeve, numbered 23, empty. Mr. Abbot's one line is in her handbag. She will not read it to us. We asked twice.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: No tin for Party Line. One of the children left her a sardine. She ate it.

lead.headline: Mrs. Grieve's capsule to be sealed at the Flushing Free Library at 11 a.m.
lead.deck: 38 records for 1978, the thirteen mothers among them; No. 23 not among them; an empty sleeve so numbered to be sealed with them; Mr. Abbot 'may attend'
lead.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve will seal the second capsule of records for 1978 at the Flushing Free Library at 11 a.m. today, the library states. It will hold 38 records, among them the thirteen mothers' records, and an empty sleeve numbered 23. Record No. 23 remains in the keeping of Mr. Cyril Abbot of the Phonautograph Society, whose reply of June 12 to Mrs. Grieve ran to 'one line.' Mr. Abbot may attend. The capsule is to be opened on June 15, 1978.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,198 night calls on the tone in Queens; 776 on the Brooklyn door
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,198 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,240, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 776. Dr. Emil Rastin's meter on 31st Street reads 41 cycles.

columns.headline: Licences: 1,881 granted; 4,690 forms returned; the ferry 'a building afloat'
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 279 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 1,881 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms, 4,690 have been returned. The Astoria ferry's saloon deck has been ruled 'a building, afloat,' and licensed.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on an eleventh Friday; nine children attend
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the eleventh Friday without one, the supervisor states. Nine schoolchildren were admitted to the parcel room and left at 5 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-eighth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 78. Saturday. Sealed till 1978. Set an alarm.

lead.headline: Grieve seals her capsule for 1978, and No. 23 is left on hold
lead.deck: Thirty-eight records and one empty sleeve go into the copper at the Flushing library; Mr. Abbot attends, stands at the back, and leaves before the solder sets
lead.body: At eleven this morning Mrs. Grieve sealed thirty-eight records for 1978 into a copper box at the Flushing Free Library, the thirteen mothers among them, and one empty sleeve with 23 written on it in her own hand. Mr. Abbot came. He stood at the back by the periodicals with his hat on and said nothing. When the solder went on he left. Mrs. Grieve did not look round. The box goes under the reading room floor. In 1978 somebody will open it and find a gap.

columns.headline: Hoover signs the farm bill, and the White House machine catches the pen
columns.body: The President signed the Agricultural Marketing Act this morning and set up a Farm Board with five hundred million dollars to spend. The White House machine recorded the pen. Queens farmers, of whom a few remain past Bayside, are advised to expect a letter.

columns.headline: Week's count: Queens rings in less, and Brooklyn's door keeps climbing
columns.body: Queens rang the Exchange about the night tone eleven hundred and ninety-eight times this week, down again. Brooklyn's door says seven hundred and seventy-six, up again. Mr. Tully says nothing, as usual, in a notice. Dr. Rastin's meter says forty-one, as usual, without one.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'What did Mr. Abbot's one line say?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator does not know, and if she did, she would not say. Mrs. Grieve has it in her handbag. Mr. Abbot has it in his head. The capsule does not have it at all. That, we suspect, is rather the point.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Feeney and Dolan go before Justice Lowry on Monday. The wire and the pencil have both been told to wear a tie.

editorial.headline: Beach censor wears the bathing costume of 1890
editorial.body: The Coney Island beach censor, Mr. Hubert Mallory, who measures the bathing costumes of young women with a tape and fines any knee he can see, was himself on the beach on Sunday in a costume of 1890: wool to the wrist, wool to the ankle, a bonnet with a veil, fastened up the back with fifty buttons and a spider in black thread, and no way to undo them. The crowd measured him. He was found in violation on eleven counts. The Speaker regrets the indignity to an officer of the beach. We have measured our sympathy with his own tape, and find it falls a little short of the knee.
